newsitem.title: USA: Clinton links clean air to school performance.
newsitem.headline: Clinton links clean air to school performance.

text.p: President Clinton linked his administration's new standards on clean air to children's academic performance Wednesday, saying students who have to live with pollution fall behind in school.
"We have to keep having a clean environment if we want healthy children," Clinton told educators and others at a conference in Nashville pushing for more family involvement in children's education.

He approved "some very strong regulations today that will be somewhat controversial, but I think kids ought to be healthy," Clinton said. "Children with asthma don't do very well in school. Children with gripping allergies that they could have avoided if they hadn't had to breathe dirty air don't do as well in school," he said. "So the public health and the environment are important parts of this."

Under the new plan, major producers of smog and soot such as big power plants would be required to meet tougher standards and violators could be severely punished. Clinton said the clean air standards he had approved would control pollution from soot and smog but would be flexible enough to allow the economy to continue to grow.

Before addressing the environment issue, he took part in a discussion with education and business leaders stressing greater involvement by communities and families in innovative school programmes. He applauded the leaders, notably those from disadvantaged schools who had worked within their communities to expand classroom space and serve their students better.

But he said, "We have an increasing divergence between the people who have money and the people who have children in the schools ... There is, I think, this underlying assumption that these kids that are in very difficult circumstances have parents that, A, can't do better than they're doing, and B, don't want to. And both those things are just false."

Among others, he listened to the experience of Yvonne Chan, principal of Vaughn Next Century Learning Centre in San Fernando, California, and Diana Lam, superintendent of the San Antonio Independent School District in Texas. Both praised the Clinton administration for cutting bureaucratic red tape and allowing them more latitude to improve their schools.

Clinton noted that while younger American children scored well on a recent international math test when compared with other countries, teenagers did poorly. He said this could be because the problems of adolescence are magnified for U.S. teenagers who grow up in poverty or under otherwise difficult circumstances.

"When a lot of these kids reach adolescence, every single problem that affects every adolescent hits them multiplied by a hundred. And we've got to find a way to keep their parents or other concerned adults involved with them when they reach adolescence," he said.
The Nashville conference was the sixth in a series of so-called Family Re-Unions organised by Vice President Al Gore and his wife Tipper Gore.

After the conference, Clinton headed for Chicago for a fund-raiser with Sen. Carol Moseley-Braun, an Illinois Democrat, and then to his boyhood home of Hope, Arkansas, where he was to attend the funeral of his great-uncle on Thursday. Clinton was then to travel to New York City for a speech to the U.N. Earth Summit.
